
F and t tests rest on the model's distributional assumptions and, for mixed models, on
approximate degrees of freedom. With few experimental units, skewed residuals or a
GLMM, resampling tests are a useful check. predictmeans has:

- `permmodels()`: permutation tests of the terms and coefficients of `lm`, `aov`, `glm`,
  `gls`, `lme`, `lmer`, `glmer` and `glmmTMB` models;
- `permlmer()` (also as `permglmer()` and `permglmmTMB()`) and `permanova.lmer()`:
  permutation likelihood-ratio tests comparing two nested mixed models, including tests
  of random effects;
- `permindex()`: permutations restricted by the design (within blocks, of whole plots),
  for randomisation tests;
- `bootmodels()`: parametric bootstrap tests for `lmer` and `glmer` models.

The results of `permmodels()` and `bootmodels()` can be passed to `predictmeans()` and
`contrastmeans()` (argument `permlist`), which then give resampling p-values for pairwise
comparisons and contrasts.

The examples below use 99 to 999 resamples so that they run quickly; use 999 or more in
practice. The smallest p-value possible is 1/(number of resamples + 1). `ncore` sets the
number of cores used for refits (`ncore = 1` here, as for CRAN checks); `seed` makes
the results reproducible without changing your own random number stream.

```{r}
library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ nitro * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)
```

## How the data are permuted

`permmodels()` has two schemes.

- **Freedman–Lane** (`method = "freedman-lane"`; the default, through `method =
  "auto"`). For each test, the model without the tested term (for a pair of means: with
  the two means equal) gives fitted values and residuals; the residuals are permuted
  and added back to those fitted values, and the statistic is computed again (Freedman
  and Lane 1983). The other terms keep their effects, so each test is of its own term.
  For linear mixed models the residuals are decorrelated with the symmetric square root
  of their covariance before they are permuted and correlated again after, and the model
  is refitted to each permuted data set, so its variance parameters are estimated again
  each time (one set of refits per term). `refit = FALSE` instead fixes the covariance
  of the data at the fit, which turns the model into a linear model with no refits:
  much faster, but slightly liberal when the variance parameters rest on few units
  (whole plots with few blocks: 8.6% instead of 5% in a simulation study, against 5.0%
  with refits). GLMs and GLMMs are first linearised at the fit (working response and
  working variances on the link scale); a GLMM is then treated as its working linear
  mixed model and refitted in the same way.
- **Raw** (`method = "raw"`, the scheme of predictmeans 1.x). The response (`lm`, `glm`)
  or the fitted values together with the decorrelated residuals (mixed models) are
  permuted, and the model is refitted to each permuted data set. The refits are kept in
  `permlist`. This scrambles the effects of all the terms at once, so it tests the
  global null hypothesis; with a covariate that has extreme values and is related to the
  tested term it rejected true null hypotheses too often (6–7% at the 5% level, against
  4–5% for Freedman–Lane, in a simulation study; Anderson and Legendre 1999 found the
  same for linear models).

```{r}
perm <- permmodels(fm, nperm = 199, seed = 1, ncore = 1)
```

For `lm`, `aov`, `lme` and `gls` models the tables are the model's own tests with a
`Perm_p_value` column; for the other classes they show the statistics that were
permuted (Wald t and F with the covariance of the data fixed at the fit).

```{r}
fm_cars <- lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
permmodels(fm_cars, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1)
```

## Pairwise comparisons and contrasts

The same permutations give p-values for pairwise comparisons, in the `pairs` table and
the legacy p-value matrix. With Freedman–Lane each pair is tested with its own reduced
model, in which that pair's means are equal, so its p-value does not depend on the other
means:

```{r}
pm <- predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = perm, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE, ncore = 1)
pm$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "statistic", "p.value", "p.method")]
```

and for contrasts:

```{r}
cm <- contrast_family(Kmatrix(fm, "nitro"), "trt.vs.ctrl")
contrastmeans(fm, "nitro", ctrmatrix = cm, permlist = perm)[[1]]
```

With `method = "raw"` all pairs use the same refits. `adj` adjusts the permutation
p-values with any `p.adjust()` method or `"sidak"`, and with the max-|t| method of
Westfall and Young (1993), which uses the correlation between the comparisons:
`adj = "tukey"` (or `"mvt"`) compares each pair's |t| with the largest |t| of the family
in each permuted data set (a permutation Tukey test), and `adj = "westfall"` does the
same step by step, which is more powerful. In a simulation study this kept the
familywise error rate as Tukey's test does.

```{r}
pmw <- predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = perm, adj = "westfall", plot = FALSE,
                    prtnum = FALSE, ncore = 1)
pmw$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "p.value", "p.adj")]
```

With a `permlist`, the
observed t statistics use the unadjusted covariance (no Kenward–Roger adjustment), as
the permuted ones do.

## GLMs and GLMMs

For GLMs and GLMMs `permmodels()` works on the working (link) scale, with the dispersion
estimated from the working residuals, which makes it much less sensitive to
overdispersion than the likelihood-ratio test. For the clinical trial data (a binomial
GLMM):

```{r}
data(Clinical)
fm_clin <- glmer(cbind(Favorable, Total - Favorable) ~ Treatment + (1 | Clinic),
                 family = binomial, data = Clinical)
perm_clin <- permmodels(fm_clin, nperm = 199, seed = 1, ncore = 1)
```

## Testing random effects: `permlmer()`

`permlmer()` compares two nested mixed models with a permutation likelihood-ratio test
(Lee and Braun 2012). This is useful for random effects, where the usual chi-square
reference distribution is wrong because the null value of a variance lies on the
boundary. Does the slope for `Days` vary between subjects?

```{r}
fm1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
fm0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
permlmer(fm0, fm1, nperm = 99, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
```

For GLMMs (`glmer` or `glmmTMB`, also as `permglmer()` and `permglmmTMB()`) the same is
done on the working scale. For 0/1 responses, where the working scale fails with rare
events or tiny clusters, randomised quantile residuals are permuted instead and the
GLMMs refitted (`method = "quantile"`, chosen automatically). Do tick counts vary between
locations, beyond the variation between broods?

```{r}
gm1 <- glmer(TICKS ~ YEAR + scale(HEIGHT) + (1 | BROOD), family = poisson,
             data = lme4::grouseticks)
gm2 <- update(gm1, . ~ . + (1 | LOCATION))
permglmer(gm1, gm2, nperm = 99, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
```

`permanova.lmer()` applies the same test to each fixed term of an `lmer` or `glmer`
model in turn (Type I, II or III), for an ANOVA table with permutation p-values.

## Permutations restricted by the design: `permindex()`

In a designed experiment the randomisation defines which permutations are possible:
treatments are randomised within blocks, whole-plot treatments to whole plots.
`permindex()` gives such permutations, and `permmodels()` and `permlmer()` use them
through `perms` (a randomisation test):

```{r}
fm_rcb <- lm(yield ~ Block + nitro, data = Oats)
idx <- permindex(Oats, block = "Block", nsim = 999, seed = 1)
permmodels(fm_rcb, perms = idx)$ANOVA
```

## Parametric bootstrap: `bootmodels()`

`bootmodels()` simulates new responses from the model fitted without its fixed effects
(an intercept and the same random effects: the global null hypothesis), refits the full
model to each and compares the statistics. For the clinical trial data:

```{r}
boot <- bootmodels(fm_clin, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
```

Its result is used as a `permlist`; the `pairs` table then says `"bootstrap"`:

```{r}
pmb <- predictmeans(fm_clin, "Treatment", permlist = boot, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE,
                    ncore = 1)
pmb$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "p.value", "p.method")]
```

## Which to use

| Model | Terms, coefficients, pairs, contrasts | Random effects, nested models |
|---|---|---|
| `lm`, `aov` | `permmodels()` (Freedman–Lane) | — |
| `glm` | `permmodels()` (Freedman–Lane on the working scale) | — |
| `lmer`, `lme`, `gls` | `permmodels()` (Freedman–Lane with refits); or the Kenward–Roger F test | `permlmer()` |
| `glmer`, `glmmTMB` | `permmodels()` (Freedman–Lane on the working scale, with refits) | `permlmer()`: working scale; quantile residuals for 0/1 responses |
| designed experiments | `permmodels(perms = permindex(...))` for a randomisation test | |

- With large samples and well-behaved residuals the F and t tests (with Kenward–Roger
  df for `lmer`) agree closely with these, at a fraction of the time.
- `bootmodels()` simulates from the global null model; it is useful as a check for GLMMs
  and very small samples.
- The choices come from simulation studies of the type I error and power of each scheme
  (in the package sources: `dev/permutation-plan.md` and `dev/sim-study/`).

## References

Anderson, M. J. and Legendre, P. (1999). An empirical comparison of permutation methods
for tests of partial regression coefficients in a linear model. *Journal of Statistical
Computation and Simulation* 62, 271–303.

Freedman, D. and Lane, D. (1983). A nonstochastic interpretation of reported
significance levels. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics* 1, 292–298.

Dunn, P. K. and Smyth, G. K. (1996). Randomized quantile residuals. *Journal of
Computational and Graphical Statistics* 5, 236–244.

Lee, O. E. and Braun, T. M. (2012). Permutation tests for random effects in linear mixed
models. *Biometrics* 68, 486–493.

Westfall, P. H. and Young, S. S. (1993). *Resampling-Based Multiple Testing*. Wiley.
